items.title: Java4Shell: critical Java flaw opens Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and others to takeover
items.why: A bug in Java's fast Base64 decoder (OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, on newer Intel/AMD chips) can let attackers run code in common apps. Oracle patched it Nov. 17; a proof of concept is public, no attacks reported yet.
items.action: Update Java on servers running Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak or similar apps; if you can't yet, start Java with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.

items.title: Google sees attackers' AI agents find and exploit web app flaws from patches on their own
items.why: Google's threat team found an AI framework that compares patched and unpatched code, then builds and runs working exploits with no human help. The gap between a patch and an attack keeps shrinking.
items.action: Apply security updates for internet-facing websites and apps within days, not weeks, and turn on automatic updates where your vendor offers them.

items.title: Apple iCloud outage traced to an internal update; Equinor reports a cyberattack
items.why: On Nov. 17 an Apple internal update knocked out iCloud sign-in, the App Store and new iPhone activation for many users. Separately, energy firm Equinor said attackers hit some IT systems, with no impact on production.
items.action: Treat surprise Apple ID password prompts during outages with care: sign in only through Settings, never from a link in an email or text.

items.title: Google Project Zero will publish bug details after 90 days, falling to 30 days by 2028
items.why: Google's bug hunters now disclose 90 days after reporting a flaw, fixed or not, dropping to 60 days in February 2027 and 30 days in January 2028. Exploited bugs get 7 days. Vendors and customers will have less time to patch.
items.action: Shorten your own patch cycle now: set a target of patching critical updates within 14 days and check monthly that it is being met.

items.title: Alleged INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate extradited to the US
items.why: A Kazakh man accused of attacks on schools, hospitals and companies in at least six states appeared in a Tennessee federal court. His group claimed 50 TB of stolen data and $500 million in ransom demands.
items.action: Keep offline or immutable backups and test a restore this month; INC and Lynx affiliates steal data first, then encrypt.

items.title: California fines Hertz $1.55 million for ignoring browser privacy opt-out signals
items.why: California's privacy agency said Hertz did not honor automatic opt-out signals from browsers and made opting out harder. Any business covered by California's privacy law must respect these signals.
items.action: Check that your website's cookie or consent tool honors Global Privacy Control signals if you serve California customers.
